title: Nano-encapsulated senolytic cocktail attenuates germ cell senescence in female mice
journal: Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences: CMLS

sections.abstract:
Low-quality oocytes directly affect fertilization and embryonic development, contributing to infertility in women, while germ cell senescence leads to reduced germ cell numbers and decreased egg quality. Dasatinib and quercetin (D and Q), as senolytic drugs, have been extensively explored in different age-related diseases. However, their effects on in vitro cultured senescent oocytes and the molecular mechanisms underpinning ovarian aging remain elusive. Here, we report that a nano-encapsulated senolytic D + Q cocktail efficiently improves the quality of post-ovulatory aging oocyte in vitro and follicle quantity in ovaries in a cyclophosphamide (Cy)-induced premature ovarian failure (POF) mouse model. Cocktail supplementation to cultured oocytes potently reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, maintains spindle integrity, decreases fragmented oocyte frequencies, rescues mislocalized cortical granules (CGs) and mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), and alleviates DNA damage and apoptosis. Importantly, the cocktail effectively ameliorates fertility deficits in the model. Transcriptome analysis shows cocktail administration to fertility-deficient mice not only up-regulates developmental gene expression but also reduces senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) accumulation. Therefore, our nano-encapsulated D + Q cocktail is a promising reagent for assisted reproductive technology and improving reproductive outcomes in POF.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00018-025-05697-7.
sections.introduction:
Infertility affects approximately 186 million individuals worldwide [ 1 ], while high infertility rates impact on population growth. Factors related to females are solely responsible for 70–80% of infertility issues [ 2 ], with the most common cause being ovarian senescence [ 3 ].

Ovarian senescence markedly reduces follicle quantities and oocyte quality in the female reproductive system, leading to premature ovarian failure (POF), which significantly impairs female fecundity [ 4 – 6 ]. POF is typically characterized by ovarian follicle loss [ 7 ]. There are two mouse models that have been used to test drug efficacy for treating POF, such as the natural aging model and the accelerated ovarian aging model [ 8 ]. Natural reproductive senescence representing follicular decrease is due to aging, while accelerated ovarian aging represents external factors which accelerate follicle depletion, like infections, ovarian surgery, genetic alterations, metabolic disorders/autoimmune diseases, and radiotherapy/chemotherapy [ 7 , 9 – 11 ]. Cyclophosphamide (Cy) is a chemotherapeutic drug and is commonly used to induce POF [ 8 , 12 ]; however, no effective treatment methods are currently available for the condition. Critically, ovarian senescence appears to be getting worse as the reproductive age of women is delayed [ 6 , 13 ]. Although assisted reproductive technology (ART) has become the main therapeutic approach for infertility, healthy oocytes are critical for correct fertilization and embryonic development [ 14 , 15 ]. During ART, oocyte retrieval can be performed by surgery and oocytes further handled in vitro [ 16 , 17 ]. With extended periods of time following ovulation, the metaphase II stage oocyte experiences deterioration in quality, referred to as post-ovulatory oocyte aging. Post-ovulatory aging occurs both in vivo and in vitro and has been associated with reduced fertilization rates, poor embryo quality, post-implantation errors and abnormalities in the offspring [ 15 , 18 ]. Post-ovulatory aging oocytes also undergo rapid aging processes [ 18 ]. Senescent oocytes are represented by dysfunctional mitochondria, increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, disordered cortical granules (CGs), and abnormal meiotic spindle and chromosome formation [ 15 , 19 – 21 ]. Thus, given oocyte aging and its impact on reproduction, effective strategies are required to alleviate female ovarian senescence.

Dasatinib (D) is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, while quercetin (Q) is a naturally occurring flavonoid. Both compounds are extensively used as senolytics to selectively eliminate senescent cells via apoptosis [ 22 ]. Their complementary mechanisms allow them to target a broader range of senescent cells compared to either agent alone. This combination has demonstrated efficacy in multiple preclinical models of aging-related diseases, and clinical trials are ongoing for various age-related pathologies [ 23 – 26 ]. Notably, the first clinical trial of D + Q in 14 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis reported significantly improved physical performance [ 27 ], and recently, a second stage trial has just ended [ 28 ]. Additionally, Hickson et al . first demonstrated that D + Q reduced senescent adipose tissue cells in patients with diabetic kidney disease [ 29 ]. Other studies have also shown that D + Q exerts beneficial effects on age-dependent intervertebral disc degeneration [ 30 ] and hepatic steatosis [ 31 ]. Despite these promising results, there are conflicting reports regarding D + Q's effects on ovarian reserve. However, its ability to reduce the senescent cell burden in ovarian tissues of obese and chemotherapy-exposed models aligns with potential benefits for POF [ 32 , 33 ]. It is suggested that improved drug delivery might resolve some of these efficacy discrepancies. Furthermore, the effects of D + Q on in vitro cultured senescent oocytes remain largely unknown. Therefore, the therapeutic potential and optimal drug delivery of D + Q in POF need to be further determined.

Here, we examined the therapeutic potential of D + Q in mice. Due to poor water solubility and to enhance drug efficacy, D + Q were encapsulated in nanoparticles (NPs). Our analyses using in vitro cultured oocytes indicated that D + Q supplementation significantly reduced ROS levels, decreased fragmented oocyte frequency, maintained spindle integrity, rescued mislocalized CGs and MMP, and alleviated DNA damage/apoptosis. Furthermore, a low nano-encapsulated D + Q cocktail dose effectively ameliorated fertility deficits in a Cy-induced POF mouse model. RNA sequencing indicated that D + Q up-regulated developmental genes that may reduce senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) accumulation. Collectively, we highlight promising therapeutic potential for D + Q in improving ART and female fecundity.
sections.methods:
Animal studies adhered to Experimental Animal Ethics Committee guidelines at our hospital. Female Institute of Cancer Research mice (6–8 weeks old) came from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology (Beijing, China), and were housed at 20–23℃ under 12/12 h light/dark cycle conditions, with ad libitum access to food/water. To generate a POF model, mice were intraperitoneally injected for 7 consecutive days with Cy (Cat #S2057, Selleck, USA) at 75 mg/kg/day or an equal volume of saline solution (control; Ctrl) [ 8 ]. For subsequent studies, mice were randomly divided into Ctrl, POF + 5% glucose solution (Cy-induced POF mice treated with 5% glucose solution, Cy), and POF + D + Q (Cy-induced POF mice treated with D + Q cocktail, D + Q) groups.

We prepared NPs using a solvent evaporation approach. Briefly, 100 mg of polycaprolactone (PCL), 10 mg of D (Cat #S1021, Selleck), 10 mg of Q (Cat #S2391, Selleck) or rhodamine b (Cat #R104960, Aladdin, China) and 40 mg of pluronic F68 (Cat #P824043, Macklin, China) were added to 5 mL of dichloromethane (DCM). After mixing with 15 mL of a 5% (w/v) polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) solution (Aladdin, China), the mixture was sonicated for 30 min on ice to allow for an oil/water emulsion to form. The DCM was removed by evaporation (stirring for up to 4 h), after which NPs were pelleted by centrifugation (11,000 g for 40 min), followed by three washes in distilled water, and final resuspension in 10 mL of 5% glucose.

Mice were injected with pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (10 IU, Cat #PCL0120, Sansheng, China) and human chorionic gonadotropin (10 IU HCG, Cat #PCL0121, Sansheng). Oocytes were then harvested from oviductal ampullae at 12–14 h after HCG injection, with cumulus cells removed by incubation with 0.3% hyaluronidase (Cat #H3506, Sigma, USA). We utilized a post-ovulatory aging oocyte model, from which fresh denuded MII oocytes cultured for 24 h in vitro can rapidly senesce in an external hyperoxic environment, distinct from naturally aged cells [ 34 ]. Fresh denuded MII oocytes were washed (at least three times) and cultured for 24 h in M2 medium (Cat #M7167, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) with/without different D or/and Q concentrations.

After fixing in 4% paraformaldehyde (30 min), permeabilizing in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) plus 0.5% Triton X-100 (PBST) (20 min) at room temperature (RT), oocytes were blocked in PBS plus 1% bovine serum albumin for 60 min at RT and incubated with α-tubulin-FITC (1:200) or γ-H2 A.X antibodies (1:200) overnight at 4℃, or a lens culinaris agglutinin (LCA)-FITC antibody (1:100) for 60 min at RT. After washing three times in PBST, oocytes were incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) or Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) antibodies for 60 min at RT, followed by 4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining for 10 min. Oocytes were then mounted on glass slides and images acquired under laser scanning confocal microscopy (Nikon, Japan).

Dichlorofluorescein (DCFH) staining and MitoTracker labeling were performed by incubating oocytes in M2 medium plus 10 mM DCFH diacetate (DCFHDA, Cat #C1062S, Beyotime, China) and 500 nM MitoTracker Red CMXRos (Cat #M7512, Invitrogen, USA), respectively. We evaluated MMP by incubating oocytes in M2 medium plus 2 mM JC-1 (MitoProbe JC-1 assay kit, Cat # M34152 , Invitrogen). Following incubation for 30 min at 37℃ in the dark (DCFH staining) or in a dark 5% CO 2 environment (MitoTracker labeling and MMP analysis), oocytes were washed three times in M2 medium and imaged under laser scanning confocal microscopy using 488 nm green fluorescence excitation for DCFH staining, 562 nm red fluorescence excitation for MitoTracker labeling, and 488 nm and 562 nm fluorescence excitation for MMP. Live oocytes were also stained with Annexin V (Annexin-V Staining kit, Cat #C1062S; Beyotime, China) at 488 nm (green fluorescence).

Ovarian tissues were lysed in RIPA buffer (Roche Diagnostics, Switzerland), added to sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) sample buffer and boiled for 10 min, proteins resolved by 10% or 12% SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Millipore, USA). Non-specific antibodies were blocked in 5% skim milk for 60 min at RT. Primary antibodies (Table S1 ) were incubated at 4 °C overnight. Then, after washing three times in TBST for 10 min each and incubating with appropriate horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies at RT for 60 min, protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence and an iBright ™ chemiluminescence imaging instrument (iBright 1500, Thermo Fisher).

After fixing in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, ovarian tissues were embedded in paraffin, from which serial sections (5 µm thick) were stained in hematoxylin/eosin (H&E). Follicles were counted (blindly) on every five sections, after which follicle numbers were multiplied by five to generate total follicle numbers at different stages.

We used a mouse XL cytokine array kit (R&D Systems, ARY028) to examine protein extracts from ovaries. Briefly, isolated ovaries were homogenized in PBS plus protease inhibitors (Cat #4693132001, Roche). Cell debris was removed by 1% Triton X-100 addition and then centrifugation (10,000 g for 5 min), after which the supernatant was used to incubate a pre-blocked membrane (array kit component) with shaking overnight at 4 °C. The membrane was then thoroughly washed three times in PBS and incubated with an antibody cocktail for at least 60 min at RT with shaking. After thorough PBS washes, streptavidin-HRP was added and the membrane incubated for 30 min at RT. Protein band detection was performed using a Chemi reagent mix (array kit component) and autoradiography.

Total RNA was isolated from ovarian tissues utilizing Trizol reagent, and subsequently reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA) with PrimeScript RT Master Mix. The synthesized cDNA was preserved at – 80 ℃ until further analysis. The qRT-PCR assays were executed with PerfectStart ® Green qPCR SuperMix on a Roche LightCycler 480 Real-Time PCR System (Cat #AQ601-03, TransGen Biotech, Beijing, China). The sequences of the oligonucleotide primers employed are detailed in Table S2 . Gene expression levels were standardized against the endogenous control Gapdh , and relative quantification of gene expression changes was calculated using the comparative CT method. All experiments were replicated three times to ensure reproducibility and reliability of the results.

For SA-β-gal activity, freshly collected ovarian tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h. Following fixation, the tissues were rinsed three times with phosphate-buffered saline containing Tween-20 (PBST) for 5 min each and subsequently immersed in a 30% sucrose solution for cryoprotection. Tissue sections of 10 µm thickness were prepared using a cryostat and stained using an SA-β-gal staining kit (Cat # CAS0030, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.

ELISA was conducted according to manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, mouse blood was collected and centrifuged to generate serum (2000 g for 15 min). Anti-mullerian hormone (AMH, Cat #ml037597, Mlbio, China) and E2 (Cat #HA009482, Shanghai ToYongBio Tech. Inc, China) serum levels were then determined on a microplate reader at 450 nm (Biotek, Cytation5).

Total RNA for bulk RNA-seq and RNA from three sets of samples (Ctrl, Cy, and D + Q three oocytes/sample) for single cell RNA-seq were isolated from ovaries using TRIzol (Invitrogen, 10296028). 1 µg RNA for RNA-seq and total RNA for single oocyte transcriptome analysis were applied for mRNA isolation by using mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (NEB, E7490). First and second cDNA synthesis steps were conducted, followed by DNA fragmentation, end repair, ‘‘A’’ addition and joint steps. For bulk RNA-seq, we constructed DNA libraries after eight PCR amplification cycles, while the single oocyte transcriptome library underwent 17 cycles. We performed high-throughput RNA sequencing on the Novaseq 6000 platform to a 1.5 × 10 7 read depth.

After removing sequencing adapters from raw reads, we aligned clean data to a human reference genome (mm10) using HISAT2 software (v.2.1.0.). We quantified gene expression by counting sequencing reads within genes and then normalized counts using edgeR. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were then identified and normalized using DESeq2, |log2 FC|> 1, and p < 0.05 thresholds. Enriched gene ontology (GO) terms were identified (MGI GO Term Finder) using log2 (fold-change) ≥ 1 and p < 0.05 thresholds.

We analyzed data from at least three independent experiments using unpaired-sample t -tests (GraphPad Prism 8), with values represented as the mean ± standard error of the mean. Significant differences were accepted at p < 0.05.

To investigate D and Q effects on oocyte senescence, oocytes were collected for different assays (Fig. 1 A). We first treated oocytes with different concentrations of D (0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5 μM) for 24 h and observed a decreased incidence of fragmented oocytes compared to aged groups when oocytes were exposed to 0.2 and 0.5 μM of D (Fig. 1 B, C ). As intracellular ROS accumulation reflects oocyte senescence, we examined ROS levels using DCFH staining and observed that ROS accumulation was unaffected at all doses (Fig. S1 A, B). Oocytes were also treated with different Q concentrations (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 μM) which indicated that fragmentation frequencies and ROS levels were unaffected (data not shown). We then screened higher Q concentrations (6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 μM). In contrast to D, ROS accumulation was significantly reduced by 7 μM Q when compared to post-ovulatory aging oocytes, while fragmentation rates were unaffected at all doses (Figs. 1 D, E and S1 C, D). Thus, D and Q exerted different delaying effects on oocyte aging; D maintained cytoplasmic integrity while Q reduced ROS accumulation. Based on our previous results, we examined optimal D (0.2 μM) and Q (7 μM) concentrations. To maximize D and Q effects in preventing senescence burden in post-ovulatory aging oocytes, an optimal D + Q dose combination was determined. We first combined different D concentrations (0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 μM) with 7 μM of Q. The cocktail, containing 0.2 μM D plus 7 μM of Q (D + Q), effectively reduced ROS levels when compared to the post-ovulatory aging oocyte group (Fig. 2 A, B ). Conversely, when different Q concentrations (7, 8, 9, and 10 μM) were combined with 0.2 μM of D, the 0.2 μM D + 7 μM Q cocktail elicited optimal effects (Fig. 2 C, D ). We next tested whether the D + Q cocktail could improve oocyte quality and resist senescence. Aberrant spindle assembly usually generates aneuploid embryos, which is an important indicator of aged oocytes; therefore, we examined spindle morphology in all groups. From immunofluorescence and quantification analyses, an increased incidence of disorganized spindle apparatus was observed in post-ovulatory aging oocytes, but this was significantly decreased by the D + Q cocktail (Fig. 2 E). As oocyte-specific vesicles, CGs migrate to cortical regions at MII stages to block polyspermy during fertilization. Thus, CG distribution can be used to evaluate oocyte quality [ 15 , 35 ]. Immunofluorescence and quantitative analyses indicated high levels of disordered CGs in the aged group but this was partially recovered in the D + Q cocktail group (Fig. 2 F), thereby improving post-ovulatory aging oocyte quality. A previous study reported that ROS accumulation occurred due to mitochondrial dysfunction [ 15 ]. Additionally, mitochondria have key roles in oocyte maturation and embryonic development [ 36 ]. To ascertain if the D + Q cocktail modulated mitochondrial function, we analyzed mitochondrial distribution patterns using MitoTracker. We observed strong signals around spindles in young oocytes; however, in contrast, only weak signals were detected in post-ovulatory aging oocytes. Interestingly, mitochondrial distribution was partially restored in the D + Q cocktail group (Fig. 3 A, B ). MMP is also an important indicator of mitochondrial function and required for respiratory activity. We next examined MMP in all groups using JC-1 staining; red fluorescence represented high MMP, whereas green fluorescence indicated low MMP (Fig. 3 C). We observed that red/green fluorescence ratios were significantly reduced in post-ovulatory aging oocytes when compared to young oocytes, but ratios were significantly recovered after D + Q cocktail treatment (Fig. 3 D). ROS accumulation is closely associated with DNA damage and apoptosis [ 15 , 37 ]. Immunofluorescence using a γ-H2AX antibody indicated elevated DNA damage incidences in post-ovulatory aging oocytes, but these were significantly reduced after D + Q cocktail treatment (Fig. 3 E, F ). By Annexin-V staining, oocyte proportions undergoing apoptosis were considerably reduced after D + Q treatment, in direct comparison to post-ovulatory aging oocytes (Fig. 3 G, H ). Therefore, aging-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis processes in oocytes were potentially alleviated by D + Q treatment. To analyze nano-encapsulated D + Q cocktail effects on reproductivity, we generated a Cy-induced POF mouse model as Cy is a chemotherapeutic drug commonly used to induce POF [ 8 ]. We then prepared NPs containing a D + Q cocktail (Fig. 4 A). To generate the model, a single Cy dose (75 mg/kg in 200 μL PBS) or PBS alone was intraperitoneally injected into female mice for 7 consecutive days. Subsequently, mice were given the D + Q cocktail (4 mg/kg of D and Q) or a 5% glucose solution once every 2 days for 24 days in total (Fig. 4 B). In vivo analyses showed that intraperitoneally injected NPs efficiently accumulated in ovarian tissues (Fig. 4 C). After D + Q treatment, ovaries were H&E-stained and showed significantly alleviated Cy-induced damage on ovarian follicles (Fig. 4 D). Specifically, D + Q treatment significantly attenuated a Cy-induced decrease in primordial, pre-antral, and antral follicle numbers (Fig. 4 E). We next investigated D + Q cocktail effects on Cy-induced mouse fertility in breeding assays. Compared to Ctrl mice, Cy-induced mice had on average reduced numbers of pups/litter, but this was significantly ameliorated by D + Q treatment (Fig. 4 F, G ). To examine if D + Q exerted long-term protective effects on the primordial follicle pool, Ctrl, Cy-induced, and D + Q treated-female mice were mated with 8-week old wild-type male mice for 4 continuous months. Breeding assays showed that the cumulative number of pups/female was significantly lower in Cy-induced mice when compared to Ctrls; however, D + Q treatment significantly improved fertility (Fig. 4 H). Western blotting indicated that D + Q treatment increased cytochrome P450 family 19 subfamily A member 1 (Cyp19a1) and follicle-stimulating hormone receptor (Fshr) expression levels, proteins associated with ovarian function; however, treatment reduced expression of the senescence-associated marker, P16 (Cdkn2a) (F i g. 4 I, J ). To further investigate fecundity in mice, anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) and estrogen (E2) serum levels were compared between D + Q and Cy-induced POF mice by ELISA (Fig. S2 A, B), which showed high AMH levels in D + Q-treated mouse ovaries when compared to Cy-induced POF mice (Fig. S2 C). Thus, the nano-encapsulated D + Q cocktail effectively improved fertility and suppressed Cy-induced aging.

SASP is a key senescence feature and represents secretory signal supply to surrounding and internal cellular environments to attract immune cells to remove senescent cells and facilitate healthy lifespans [ 38 , 39 ]. Considering potential D + Q cocktail actions in antagonizing ovary aging, we prepared three independent samples for RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) under different conditions to investigate if treatment influenced genome-wide transcriptome profiles, especially SASP expression (Fig. S3 A). Overall, the transcriptome showed extensive changes upon Cy-induced POF; in particular, the expression of several well-known SASP-associated genes, including Ccl2 , Cxcl10 , Vegfa , Fgf1 , Igfbp2, and Il1rn , was significantly elevated, while the expression of a development-related genes (DRGs) subset was down-regulated after POF (Fig. 5 A). Accordingly, multiple SASP-mediated immune response pathways were enriched in POF up-regulated genes, while gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA) showed that cell-cycle checkpoints and cytokine-related signaling were enriched upon Cy treatment, suggesting the rewiring of a SASP-associated gene subset following POF (Fig. S3 B). In particular, hierarchical clustering analyses showed distinct transcriptome patterns in mice after nano-encapsulated D + Q treatment. Notably, multiple signaling processes associated with SASP secretion, including growth factor regulation, cytokine secretion, and NF-κB signaling, were enriched in down-regulated genes when comparing cocktail treatments with POF; meanwhile, many development-related pathways were also re-activated, emphasizing regained growth and delayed ovary senescence processes after D + Q cocktail treatment (Fig. S3 C). While bulk RNA-seq analyses average global gene expression, RNA is more susceptible to micro- or macro-environmental stimuli/influences [ 40 ]. Thus, given considerable transcriptional diversity at single cell levels, germ cells must be independently analyzed at transcriptome levels. Therefore, we performed single-cell transcriptome oocyte analyses under different conditions (Fig. S3 D). Similar to bulk RNA-seq data, a SASP gene subset (including Cxcl5 , Mmp9 , Bcl2l2 , Igfbp5 , and Fgf1 ) was increased after Cy stimulation, accompanied by extensive DRG collapse (Fig. 5 B). Down-regulated genes were implicated in development-related pathways, while up-regulated genes were mainly enriched in SASP-mediated immune responses, thereby suggesting that a SASP gene subset had been rewired upon POF (Figs. 5 C and S3 E).

To further underscore gene set redistribution/changes after treatment with nano-encapsulated D + Q, we compared DEG dynamics under different conditions. Of note, hierarchical clustering analyses of the nano-encapsulated D + Q treatment group, by bulk RNA-seq and single oocyte transcriptome analysis, showed a remarkable recovery when compared to the gene distribution in Cy-stimulated mice (Fig. 5 D, E ). For example, expression of the senescence marker Cdkn2a and the representative SASP gene Cxcl5 was decreased after D + Q treatment (Fig. 5 D, E ). In a single oocyte, several biosynthetic pathways, crucial for development processes, were observed in nano-encapsulated D + Q up-regulated genes (Fig. S3 F); e.g., Cy-down-regulated Tgfß1 and Mapk3 genes which are developmentally implicated in TGF-β and MAPK pathways, but their levels were increased after D + Q treatment, consistent with restored growth capacity (Fig. 5 D, E ). The relative expression levels of Cdkn2a and Cyp19a1 mRNA were also examined, and Cdkn2a levels significantly decreased after D + Q treatment, while Cyp19a1 expression increased compared to the Cy-treated group (Fig. S3 G, H). Additionally, p16 (senescence marker) immunofluorescence levels had collapsed after D + Q treatment (Fig. 5 F); meanwhile, a notable decrease in the number of SA-β-gal-positive cells was observed in the ovaries of mice that had undergone D + Q treatment, highlighting senolytic cocktail actions in antagonizing ovary senescence (Figs. 5 G and S3 I). To further investigate if DRGs and SASP gene subsets were impacted in bulk RNA-seq after D + Q cocktail treatment, we measured fluctuations in DRGs and SASP-related gene expression using a defined gene list from GeneCards. DRG expression was prominently down-regulated in the POF group but rescued upon D + Q treatment (Fig. 5 H). For comparison, a SASP-related gene subset showed the opposite (F i g. 5 I). Accordingly, in a single oocyte, many SASP genes were down-regulated following senolytic cocktail treatment, which was distinct to the unchanged expression of several randomly selected genes (Fig. S3 J). Since SASP is induced by several factors, both soluble and insoluble, that can alter the cellular environment, we next examined the senescent cell secretome using commercially available cytokine arrays. Importantly, among up-regulated SASP-related genes in the POF group, we observed elevated cytokine expression, while ovaries treated with D + Q showed strongly reduced cytokine expression (Figs. 5 J and S3 K). Therefore, the nano - encapsulated senolytic cocktail D + Q effectively reduced POF-induced SASP-related gene expression and cytokine secretion, thus antagonizing senescent processes.
sections.discussion:
Human oocytes, sperm, and embryos can be handled in vitro during assisted ART [ 17 , 41 ]. However, prolonged culture may mean that oocytes can enter senescence, which affects fertilization and subsequent embryonic development [ 18 ]. ART success rates depend on methods which effectively prevent or delay oocyte aging. In this study, we showed that a D + Q cocktail effectively ameliorated low quality of post-ovulatory aging oocytes by regulating multiple cellular processes, such as ROS levels, fragmentation frequency, spindle integrity, CG localization, MMP, and DNA damage and apoptosis. Importantly, we identified different D and Q functions implicated in in vitro oocyte senescence. D sustained oocyte cytoplasmic integrity, while Q reduced ROS accumulation. Moreover, our investigation revealed a non-linear dose–response relationship between drug concentration and therapeutic outcomes. D exposure at 0.2 and 0.5 μM significantly reduced fragmented oocyte incidence in aged models. In contrast, only 7 μM Q effectively attenuated ROS accumulation in post-ovulatory aging oocyte. Notably, the combination of 0.2 μM D + 7 μM Q uniquely demonstrated optimal therapeutic effects, suggesting a dose-dependent synergy (Fig. 2 ). Meanwhile, higher concentrations may induce paradoxical effects via ROS overproduction, which counteracts anti-senescence benefits by exacerbating oxidative stress. This is further complicated by the limited toxicological data available for acute quercetin exposure, which necessitates cautious dose titration to avoid unintended adverse effects. For instance, Miao et al . showed that high-dose nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), a famous senolytic drug, reduced the number of matured oocytes in NMN treatment aged mice [ 15 ], while Yue et al . found that epitalon concentrations above 1 mM unexpectedly did not rescue the ROS accumulation in the post-ovulatory aging oocytes [ 18 ]. These studies collectively underscore the necessity of precision dosing to balance senolytic activity and off-target toxicity which need to be further evaluated. The D + Q cocktail (0.2 μM D + 7 μM Q) improved oocyte quality, and may potentially improve ART efficiency.

It was previously reported that the D + Q combination ameliorated age-related conditions, such as hepatic steatosis and intervertebral disc degeneration, and also extended lifespans in mice [ 30 , 31 , 42 ]. Hickson et al . reported that D + Q efficiently improved diabetic kidney disease symptoms in humans [ 29 ], demonstrating promising therapeutic potential for these senolytic cocktails in human diseases. POF is one of the leading causes of female infertility and one of the most severe chemotherapy side-effects in young females with cancer [ 8 ]. POF is caused by the premature aging of germ cells in the ovaries, with currently no effective treatments for the disease [ 9 , 10 , 43 ]. Importantly, two mouse models have been developed to test for drug efficacy against POF: natural aging and chemotherapy-induced mouse models [ 8 ]. As young women are the main child bearers in society, a chemotherapy-induced POF model in young female mice, and not naturally aging mice, better reflected this in our study. Cy is a chemotherapy drug commonly used for POF induction [ 44 ]. Previous studies have reported the beneficial effects of D (5 mg/kg) + Q (50 mg/kg) in ovarian injury or POF, but other studies have also reported that the D + Q treatment fails to improve ovarian reserves or fertility in female mice [ 32 , 45 , 46 ]. Since D and Q have poor water solubility, they can only be administered by gavage; therefore, data discrepancies between such studies can arise due to drug delivery or bioavailability issues. With rapid nanotechnology developments, NP-mediated delivery systems have emerged as promising therapeutics for multiple diseases [ 29 – 31 ]. These approaches increase the water solubility of candidate molecules, enhance pharmacokinetic drug properties and tissue distribution, and provide sustained drug release, thus reducing toxicity and improving therapeutic effects [ 47 ]. In our study, we successfully prepared NPs containing a D + Q cocktail and administered them (4 mg/kg of D and Q) to a Cy-induced POF mouse model via intraperitoneal injection. The cocktail not only repaired ovarian damage and inhibited follicular apoptosis, but it also improved fertility. Also, RNA-seq of mouse ovaries identified significant increases in ovarian functional genes and decreased SASP-related protein expression in D + Q-treated mice. These results suggest that a NP senolytic cocktail D + Q achieved excellent treatment outcomes in a Cy-induced POF mouse model. Thus, NP-mediated delivery systems can improve D + Q drug efficacy, and provide an important platform for future POF treatment.

Collectively, we showed that a NP senolytic cocktail alleviated germ cell aging to improve oocyte quality both in vitro and in vivo. In particular, a low NP cocktail dose produced better effects. Overall, our therapeutic platform may improve fertility under POF conditions and maintain high-quality oocytes for ART in females with infertility issues.
